blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Subordinate Courts operate at the district level under the administrative supervision and control of the State High Court.
District Judges are appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court, requiring at least 7 years of legal practice.
High Courts exercise complete administrative control (postings, promotions, discipline) over subordinate courts as per Article 235.
A death sentence awarded by a Sessions Court must be confirmed by the High Court before execution.
Lok Adalats function under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, and their awards/decisions are final and binding.

blocks.content: Subordinate Courts form the lowest tier of the Indian judicial system. They work below the High Courts and deal with the majority of cases in the country.
These courts are called 'Subordinate Courts' because they function under the control and supervision of the High Courts.
They play a very important role because common people directly interact with these courts for justice.
CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISIONS RELATED TO SUBORDINATE COURTS
The provisions related to Subordinate Courts are mentioned in Part VI of the Indian Constitution (Articles 233 to 237).

items:
• Article 233 – Appointment of District Judges
  • Article 234 – Recruitment of Judicial Officers
  • Article 235 – Control of High Court over Subordinate Courts
  • Article 236 – Interpretation
  • Article 237 – Application to certain states
Article 235 – Control of High Court over Subordinate Courts

blocks.content: Subordinate Courts are courts which are subordinate to the High Court. They include:

items:
• District Courts
  • Sessions Courts
  • Civil Courts
  • Criminal Courts
  • Revenue Courts
  • Family Courts
  • Lok Adalats (under Legal Services Authorities Act)
Lok Adalats (under Legal Services Authorities Act)

blocks.content: The hierarchy of courts in a State is as follows:
District Court is the highest court at the district level.
The District Court is the highest judicial authority in a district. It deals with:

items:
• Civil cases (as District Judge)
  • Criminal cases (as Sessions Judge)

blocks.content: The District Judge is the head of all subordinate courts in the district.
District Judges are appointed by the Governor of the State in consultation with:

items:
• Must be an advocate or pleader for at least 7 years
  • Recommended by the High Court
Must be an advocate or pleader for at least 7 years

items:

Lok Adalats are established under Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987. They aim to:

items:
• Provide free legal aid
  • Settle disputes amicably
  • Reduce burden on courts

items:
• Control of High Court

Article 233 vs Article 234: District Judges are appointed under Art. 233 (Governor + High Court), whereas Subordinate Judicial Officers are recruited under Art. 234 (Governor + High Court + State Public Service Commission).
Death Sentence Confirmation: A Sessions Court can pass a death sentence, but it cannot be executed without High Court confirmation.
Qualifications for District Judge: Candidate must be an advocate or pleader for at least 7 years and recommended by the High Court.
Article 235 Control: High Court holds exclusive administrative control (posting, promotion, leave) over subordinate courts to maintain judicial independence.

blocks.content: Subordinate Courts are the backbone of the Indian judicial system.
They directly serve the people and ensure justice at the grassroots level. Strengthening subordinate courts is essential for speedy justice and strong democracy.
